issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be refused where the agreement’s terms, the parties’ conduct, and the circumstances in which it was made give the purchaser an unfair advantage or make enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a decree ordering specific performance of an agreement to sell property for a total consideration of ₹1.6 lakh, of which ₹60,000 had been paid in advance and ₹1 lakh remained payable.
The purchaser’s father, who entered into the agreement and testified in support of the claim, carried on a moneylending business.
The sellers consistently maintained that the agreement had been executed as security for a loan; a defence witness testified that the agreement was signed in connection with repayment of a loan.
The sellers produced evidence of the property’s value, including evidence that it was valued at ₹6.3 lakh in 2006 and a document concerning its value in 1999.
Although the trial and appellate courts referred to this evidence, they did not take the relevant circumstances into account when deciding whether to grant specific performance.

The sellers offered ₹10 lakh in lieu of specific performance. The Court substituted compensation of ₹15 lakh, payable within two months, with interest at 9 per cent per annum thereafter until payment or realization.
issues.conclusion: The terms of the agreement, the parties’ conduct, and the circumstances in which it was made gave the purchaser an unfair advantage and made enforcement inequitable. The decree for specific performance was set aside and replaced with a direction to pay ₹15 lakh in compensation in lieu of specific performance, with interest at 9 per cent per annum after two months until payment or realization.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20(1) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, specific performance is discretionary, and that discretion must be sound, reasonable, and guided by judicial principles. Section 20(2)(a) and (c) permit the court to refuse specific performance where the agreement’s terms, the parties’ conduct, or the circumstances give the plaintiff an unfair advantage or make enforcement inequitable. The explanations to Section 20 clarify that mere inadequacy of consideration, an onerous contract, or an increase in property value is not by itself sufficient; the circumstances must be considered as a whole. The Court relied on Parakunnan Veetill Joseph’s Son Mathew v. Nedumbara Kuruvila’s Son, Sardar Singh v. Smt. Krishna Devi, K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd., Lourdu Mari David v. Louis Chinnaya Arogiaswamy, A.C. Arulappan v. Smt. Ahalya Naik, and Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation (P) Ltd.

rule.if: specific_performance_decree_appeal and moneylending_relationship and loan_transaction_defense_supported and price_below_documented_value and lower_courts_omitted_equitable_assessment

predicates.specific_performance_decree_appeal: The matter was an appeal from a decree ordering specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.moneylending_relationship: The purchaser’s father, who entered into the agreement, carried on a moneylending business.
predicates.loan_transaction_defense_supported: The sellers consistently asserted that the agreement was connected to a loan, and a witness testified that it was signed in connection with repayment of a loan.
predicates.price_below_documented_value: The agreed sale price was substantially below the property value indicated by evidence produced by the sellers.
predicates.lower_courts_omitted_equitable_assessmen: The lower courts referred to evidence about the transaction and property value but did not take those circumstances into account in deciding whether to grant specific performance.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a specific-performance decree involves a moneylending relationship, supported evidence that the agreement was connected to a loan, a sale price substantially below documented property value, and lower courts that omitted an equitable assessment of those circumstances, the decree is replaced with compensation.
